title_en: Homily on Not Clinging to Worldly Things
author: Basil of Caesarea
occasion: Basil exhorts his congregation not to cling to worldly goods and comforts, and responds to a recent fire that the devil stirred up against the church's precincts, which divine grace turned back before it could reach the sanctuary.
argument: Basil urges his hearers to treat this life as a road on which the devil sets ambushes through worldly pleasures, wealth, power, and bodily indulgence. He argues that only the soul and the body, together with virtues, are truly our own possessions, while riches and luxuries are alien and cannot accompany us beyond death. He calls the congregation to lighten the soul's load by giving to the poor, especially those harmed by the recent fire, and to imitate Job's patient endurance of loss. Finally, he interprets the fire as a defeated assault by the devil and encourages the survivors to turn their suffering into a crown of endurance.

outline.move: Basil opens by praising the congregation's love of correction and warns that the devil uses worldly pleasures as ambushes along the road of life.
He develops the image of life as a road and urges hearers to travel lightly and without turning aside to deceptive pleasures.
He laments that people rejoice at growing older while failing to see life being spent, and that they gather heavy earthly goods instead of light, lasting ones.
He shows that fields, houses, power, food, and sexual indulgence are all alien and passing, while the true human possession is soul and body.
He contrasts virtues, which accompany us to heaven, with wealth and luxury, which cannot, and urges care for the soul and moderate care for the body.
He compares unloading worldly goods to sailors throwing cargo overboard in a storm, and urges giving wealth to the poor as safe treasure.
He rebukes the congregation for spending on flatterers and entertainers while despising the poor, and introduces the recent fire outside the church.
He describes the fire as a devilish attack that was turned back, and calls the congregation to comfort and support those who lost everything.
He presents Job as a model of endurance, recounting his losses and his reply to his wife's despairing counsel.
He completes the portrait of Job's patience and restoration, and applies the lesson to those harmed by the recent fire.

cast.name: Basil of Caesarea
cast.who: The preacher and bishop addressing his congregation.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: The Old Testament righteous man held up as the model of patient endurance.

cast.name: Job's wife
cast.who: She urges Job to curse God and die, and is rebuked by him.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The psalmist and prophet quoted on life as a road and on God's help.

cast.name: Solomon
cast.who: The wise author quoted on reproving the wise and on fleeing a woman's face.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle quoted on the inner renewal and on contentment with food and covering.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: The patriarch whose help the rich man will beg for in vain.

cast.name: Lazarus
cast.who: The poor man from the Gospel parable, representing the needy lying before the congregation.

cast.name: the rich man
cast.who: The unmerciful rich man from the Gospel parable, whom Basil says his hearers surpass in wickedness.

voices.speaker: Basil (preacher)
voices.how_marked: The main voice of the homily, speaking in the first person singular and plural.

voices.speaker: Scripture (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'he says' or 'it is written', or woven into the argument as direct quotation.

voices.speaker: Job (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as what Job said or as words Basil puts in Job's mouth.

voices.speaker: Job's wife (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as her words to Job, reported by Basil.

voices.speaker: those who lived well (imagined speech)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as what each of those who lived well will say to the unmerciful at the judgment.

key_terms.sense: Worldly things, the affairs and possessions belonging to this present life.
The road or journey of human life, used throughout as the controlling image.
The devil, the enemy of truth who ambushes people through worldly pleasures.
Wealth, especially earthly riches that cannot be kept or carried beyond death.
Pleasures, especially deceptive worldly enjoyments used by the devil as bait.
The soul, the true possession of a human being, which must be kept pure and light.
The body, given as the soul's vehicle for life on earth and needing only moderate care.
Virtues, the lasting possessions that accompany a person to heaven.
Patient endurance, especially Job's steadfastness under suffering.
Patient endurance under trial, the virtue by which Job gained his reward.
Hell, the place of punishment awaiting the unmerciful rich.
The recent fire outside the church, understood as an attack by the devil.
The church, both the building threatened by the fire and the gathered community.
Vanities, the empty and passing things of this world.

scripture: Basil quotes the Septuagint, using Greek forms of Old Testament books and the Septuagint Psalm numbering. In a modern translation, cite these as the corresponding Hebrew Bible books and use standard modern Psalm numbering where the Septuagint numbering differs.
uncertain: The precise date of the homily.
The exact location and circumstances of the fire outside the church.
Whether the homily was delivered in Caesarea or elsewhere.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the devil stirred up against the church's precincts
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Γείτονα μὲν γὰρ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὁ δυσμενὴς ἀνῆψε πυράν
_unresolved_facts.fix: the devil kindled a fire neighboring/adjacent to the Church, not against the church's precincts specifically

_unresolved_facts.claim: divine grace turned back before it could reach the sanctuary
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ Σωτὴρ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν ἀνάψαντα ταύτην ῥυῆναι πεποίηκε, καὶ συστεῖλαι τὴν μανίαν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἑαυτὸν πάλιν προσέταξε
_unresolved_facts.fix: the Savior made it flow back upon the one who kindled it and ordered its fury to be contracted back upon itself

_unresolved_facts.claim: only the soul and the body, together with virtues, are truly our own possessions
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τί δὲ ὄντως ἡμέτερον; Ψυχή τε, ᾗ ζῶμεν, λεπτή τις οὖσα καὶ νοερά, καὶ οὐδὲν δεομένη τῶν βαρυνόντων· καὶ σῶμα, τὸ ταύτῃ δοθὲν ὄχημα πρὸς τὸν βίον παρὰ τοῦ κτίσαντος
_unresolved_facts.fix: the soul and the body given as its vehicle; virtues are later said to become our possessions when woven into nature by care

_unresolved_facts.claim: He rebukes the congregation for spending on flatterers and entertainers while despising the poor, and introduces the recent fire outside the church
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἤδη πρὸς λιμένας ἡμῖν, ὡς ὁρᾶτε, καταχθέντα τὸν λόγον, εἰς τὸν τῆς συμβουλῆς δρόμον αὖθις ἀδελφοί τινες ἐπανάγουσι, μὴ παραδραμεῖν τὰ χθὲς ὑπὸ τοῦ Δεσπότου θαυματουργηθέντα κελεύοντες
_unresolved_facts.fix: The fire is introduced in section 7 only after Basil had already concluded his main exhortation ("already as you see the word has been brought to harbor"), brought back by brothers who urge him not to pass over yesterday's miracles

_unresolved_facts.claim: He describes the fire as a devilish attack that was turned back, and calls the congregation to comfort and support those who lost everything
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ ὅπερ ἂν ἀποῤῥίψωσιν, εὐθέως ἀπώλεσαν... ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐφ' ὅσον ἂν τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξαντλήσωμεν φόρτον, πλείονα καὶ βελτίονα ταῖς ψυχᾶις πλοῦτον ἐπισωρεύσομεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 8's call to support fire victims is framed as making the devil's wound more grievous, not merely comfort; the economic metaphor of unloading/transferring wealth continues from section 6

_unresolved_facts.claim: Job's wife ... urges Job to curse God and die
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸ τῆς τοῦ κτίσαντος ὀργῆς ἀκονήσαντα ξίφος, ἢ διακαρτεροῦντα πρὸς τὰ δεινά, τὸν ἐν τοῖς ἀγῶσι μόχθον ἑαυτῷ καὶ τῇ συνοικούσῃ μηκύνειν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Job's wife urges him to cut himself off from the earth by impious words, sharpening the Creator's sword of wrath, or alternatively to prolong their suffering by enduring—she does not explicitly say 'curse God and die'

_unresolved_facts.claim: the rich man ... whom Basil says his hearers surpass in wickedness
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Δέδοικα δὲ ἐγὼ, μὴ καὶ πικροτέροις ἡμᾶς τούτων βάλωσι ῥήμασιν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ νικῶμεν ἐκεῖνον, ὡς ἴστε, τῇ πονηρίᾳ τὸν πλούσιον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Basil says his hearers surpass the rich man in wickedness (τῇ πονηρίᾳ), not that they surpass him in general

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἴπατε πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς ἅπερ ἐκεῖνος· Ὁ Κύριος ἔδωκεν, ὁ Κύριος ἀφείλετο
_unresolved_facts.fix: In section 8, Basil tells the fire survivors to say to themselves what Job said—this is Basil's voice directing, not Job quoted directly; direct Job quotations begin in section 9

_unresolved_facts.claim: those who lived well (imagined speech) ... sections ["6"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐρεῖ δὲ ἕκαστος ἐκείνων ἡμῖν κεκραγώς· Μὴ ζήτει φιλανθρωπίαν, ἣν αὐτὸς ἐφ' ἑτέρων ἠγνόησας
_unresolved_facts.fix: These are explicitly 'each of those who lived well' (ἕκαστος ἐκείνων τῶν βεβιωκότων καλῶς), not merely 'those who lived well' in general; and they speak to the unmerciful at judgment, which is more specific than 'imagined speech' suggests
